clue.text: George Villiers resisting ranter

parts.note: a horse bucking is fighting off its rider, resisting control
a ham is an actor who rants and overplays every line

explanation.surface: A courtier is pictured standing firm against a loud-mouthed agitator.
explanation.walkthrough: George Villiers was the name of the first and second Dukes of Buckingham, favourites of James I and Charles II.
explanation.definitionFit: Villiers held the dukedom whose title is this place name, so he is known by it.

clue.text: Sculptor of Carlyle starts brilliantly on his marble

indicators.note: the starts of the following four words are taken, one initial from each

explanation.surface: A sculptor of the Scottish sage makes a brilliant beginning on his marble block.
explanation.walkthrough: Joseph Edgar Boehm (spelt here without the E) made the seated statue of Thomas Carlyle on the Chelsea Embankment in London.
explanation.definitionFit: Boehm was the Victorian sculptor who carved the well-known figure of the writer Carlyle.

clue.text: Jonson's was altered

parts.note: Ben Jonson wrote a comedy titled 'The --- is Altered'; the clue gives the title with its noun missing

explanation.surface: Something belonging to the playwright Ben Jonson has been changed.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word completes the title of Jonson's comedy about a lawsuit-like situation that has changed.

clue.text: Disorganised, chaotic Simon opposes holy images

definitions.note: the definition describes what such a person does; the answer is the person who does it

indicators.note: disorganised means put out of order, so the following words have their letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A muddled man called Simon sets himself against sacred pictures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disorganised' rearranges CHAOTIC SIMON into a word for an image-fighter, an iconoclast.
explanation.definitionFit: An iconomachist is a combatant against icons, someone hostile to religious pictures.

clue.text: Roman jurist happy in France and America

parts.note: the French word for happy or cheerful is gai
US is the usual abbreviation for the United States of America

explanation.surface: A Roman lawyer is content both in France and in the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: Gaius was the second-century jurist whose Institutes are a foundation text of Roman law.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaius is the classical legal writer best known among the lawyers of ancient Rome.

clue.text: Tsarevna presented in Bolton

definitions.meaning: a tsarevna is a daughter of a Russian tsar, here the youngest daughter of Nicholas II
the playwright Guy Bolton adapted the play about the woman claiming to be the lost grand duchess

explanation.surface: A Russian princess makes an appearance in a Lancashire town.
explanation.walkthrough: Bolton looks like the Lancashire mill town, but it is Guy Bolton, who wrote the English version of the stage play later filmed with Ingrid Bergman.
explanation.definitionFit: Grand Duchess Anastasia was a tsar's daughter, and her name titles the play Bolton adapted.

clue.text: Secure accommodation for minimalist

definitions.meaning: a barred enclosure is lodging from which nothing escapes
John ... was an American composer associated with minimalism, famous for the silent piece 4'33"

explanation.surface: A locked-down lodging is offered to someone who likes very little.
explanation.definitionFit: A barred enclosure keeps its occupant secure, and the composer John Cage is a byword for spare music.

clue.text: Nothing delayed support for a job implying leadership of a Propaganda committee

indicators.note: in a down clue the support is placed below, so this pair sits under the first pair

parts.note: taken as written
a post is a job or position
O, the round figure zero, stands for nothing
something delayed is late

explanation.surface: A man who arrived late fails to back a role leading a body that spreads the faith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'support for' in a down clue puts O + LATE under A + POST. The Propaganda is the Vatican's Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith, which directs missionary work.
explanation.definitionFit: An apostolate is the office of an apostle, a mission leading the spread of the faith.

clue.text: Live practical acquaintance with theme of Blake songs

definitions.meaning: to live through something is to undergo it personally
knowledge gained by doing, rather than by reading
William Blake paired his Songs of Innocence with Songs of a second, darker state

explanation.surface: Getting to know Blake's lyrics in practice brings them to life.
explanation.definitionFit: To undergo something is to live it, the knowledge it leaves is practical familiarity, and Blake set innocence against that worldly knowing.

clue.text: Like Sabatini's Nights

parts.note: Rafael Sabatini wrote a collection titled 'The --- Nights' Entertainment', true tales from the past

explanation.surface: Something is compared to evenings spent with the swashbuckling novelist Sabatini.
explanation.definitionFit: Sabatini's collection retold real events from the past, so its nights are of that kind.

clue.text: Coward seemed to associate it with detail

definitions.text: Coward seemed to associate it with detail

parts.words: Coward seemed to associate it with detail
parts.note: Noel Coward's only novel is '... and Circumstance', and circumstance can mean detail

explanation.surface: A timid person apparently links something to the finer points.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coward' is not a timid person but Noel Coward; 'circumstance' in the old sense of detail is paired with the answer in the title of his novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Ceremonial splendour is what stands alongside circumstance in the familiar phrase Coward used as a title.

clue.text: Actors with monarch on crossing in administrative centre

parts.note: the cast is the company of actors in a production
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the monarch's cipher
a bridge is a crossing over a river or road

explanation.surface: A troupe of actors and the Queen are on a bridge in a county town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' sets ER above BRIDGE in the down entry. Casterbridge is Thomas Hardy's fictional county town in The Mayor of Casterbridge.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardy's Casterbridge, modelled on Dorchester, is the county town where the business of Wessex is run.

clue.text: Siegfried Sassoon bitterly wonders if it is significant

definitions.text: Siegfried Sassoon bitterly wonders if it is significant

parts.words: Siegfried Sassoon bitterly wonders if it is significant
parts.note: Sassoon's war poem asks this question with savage irony about soldiers losing legs, sight and sanity

explanation.surface: The war poet asks, with some bitterness, whether something counts for anything.
explanation.definitionFit: The question of whether something is significant is the title of Sassoon's ironic 1917 poem.

clue.text: Painting genre surprisingly fills islet

definitions.note: the genre is named by the plural of its works, pictures of fruit, flowers and objects

indicators.note: something turning out surprisingly comes out in an unexpected form, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An art form unexpectedly crowds a tiny island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surprisingly' rearranges FILLS ISLET; note the plural, not still lives.
explanation.definitionFit: Paintings of arranged inanimate objects form a recognised category of art.

clue.text: Order first name of Lara's creator

definitions.meaning: a religious order, the Cistercian monks named after St Bernard
Lara (1997) is a novel in verse by the British writer ... Evaristo

explanation.surface: Someone demands to be told the given name of the author of Lara.
explanation.walkthrough: Lara's creator is not Pasternak, whose Lara is in Doctor Zhivago, nor Byron's poem: it is Evaristo's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Monks of St Bernard's reform are so called, and the novelist Evaristo bears the same name.

clue.text: Colin McInnes's Absolute Beginners

parts.note: MacInnes's 1959 novel is about the young people of late-1950s London, a newly invented social group

explanation.surface: The title of Colin MacInnes's London novel is offered by itself.
explanation.definitionFit: MacInnes's novel portrays youngsters in their late adolescence, the absolute beginners of his title.

clue.text: Morse code?

parts.note: Inspector Morse kept his first name secret; it is revealed in the novels and was the title of the prequel series

explanation.surface: A question about the dot-and-dash telegraph system.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Morse code' suggests telegraphy, but the code here is the detective's hidden first name, a secret he guarded closely.
explanation.definitionFit: Colin Dexter's Inspector Morse was christened with this name, which he hid like a code word.

clue.text: Perhaps it led a 19

definitions.note: refers to the answer at 19 across, a mark over a letter

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters might be in a different order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Perhaps something took the lead in another entry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' rearranges IT LED. The answer is the wavy mark of Spanish n, an example of the answer to 19.
explanation.definitionFit: The wavy sign over n in Spanish is one of the accent marks that change a letter's sound.

clue.text: Manet and Burroughs depicted the bare fact of it

definitions.text: Manet and Burroughs depicted the bare fact of it

parts.words: Manet and Burroughs depicted the bare fact of it
parts.note: Manet painted Le Dejeuner sur l'herbe, with a nude woman, and William Burroughs wrote Naked ---

explanation.surface: A painter and a novelist each showed something stripped to its bare truth.
explanation.walkthrough: Burroughs explained his title as the frozen moment when everyone sees what is on the end of every fork; Manet's picnic has a naked woman at the meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Manet's picnic and Burroughs's novel both name a midday meal, one painted with a nude, one called naked.

clue.text: Dreadful reviewer reportedly used to modify sound

indicators.note: reportedly means as it would be heard said, so the phrase is taken by its sound

parts.note: dreadful means dire and a reviewer is a critic, giving dire critic

explanation.surface: A terrible reviewer was apparently employed to tweak the audio.
explanation.definitionFit: An accent mark placed on a letter is used to change how the letter is pronounced.

clue.text: "Thou shalt find a king that will revenge —'s death" (Henry IV Part I)

definitions.text: "Thou shalt find a king that will revenge —'s death" (Henry IV Part I)

parts.words: "Thou shalt find a king that will revenge —'s death" (Henry IV Part I)
parts.note: at Shrewsbury the Earl of Douglas kills Sir Walter Blunt disguised as the king, and Blunt tells him a real king will avenge an earlier victim

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare's Henry IV Part 1 promises royal vengeance for a death.
explanation.definitionFit: The nobleman slain at Shrewsbury while dressed as King Henry is the one whose death Blunt says will be avenged.

clue.text: Bogus, like Mozart's gardener

definitions.meaning: Mozart's opera La --- giardiniera is about a noblewoman disguised as a gardener

explanation.surface: Mozart's garden worker is a fraud.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian adjective meaning pretended describes the heroine of Mozart's opera, a sham gardener.

clue.text: "The beautiful little — had nothing for it but her attractive soul-case" (H. B. Stowe, Oldtown Folks)

definitions.text: "The beautiful little — had nothing for it but her attractive soul-case" (H. B. Stowe, Oldtown Folks)

parts.words: "The beautiful little — had nothing for it but her attractive soul-case" (H. B. Stowe, Oldtown Folks)
parts.note: Stowe's narrator dismisses a pretty girl as a deception, her lovely body hiding no soul worth the name

explanation.surface: A quotation from Harriet Beecher Stowe's novel describes a pretty girl with only her looks to offer.
explanation.definitionFit: Stowe calls the girl a fraud or deception, since her charm is all on the surface.

clue.text: Canal flows uphill for god

indicators.note: in a down clue, flowing uphill means running from the bottom upwards, so the canal's name is read backwards

parts.note: the Suez Canal links the Mediterranean and the Red Sea

explanation.surface: Water in a canal runs upwards in honour of a deity.
explanation.definitionFit: Zeus was the king of the Greek gods on Olympus.

clue.text: Just like Rosamond

definitions.meaning: Rosamond Clifford, mistress of Henry II

explanation.surface: Something is merely in the manner of a woman called Rosamond.
explanation.definitionFit: Being even-handed is being just, and the legendary mistress of Henry II is called by this epithet.

clue.text: She touched John Ridd with "sudden delight"

definitions.text: She touched John Ridd with "sudden delight"

parts.words: She touched John Ridd with "sudden delight"
parts.note: John Ridd is the narrator of R. D. Blackmore's Exmoor romance, who falls for the girl he meets as a boy in the Doone valley

explanation.surface: A woman stirs a man with a burst of joy.
explanation.definitionFit: Blackmore's heroine is the girl whose sight fills John Ridd with sudden delight.

clue.text: Penman brother of Shaunn the Post

definitions.text: Penman brother of Shaunn the Post

parts.words: Penman brother of Shaunn the Post
parts.note: in Joyce's Finnegans Wake the twin sons are the writer figure called the Penman and Shaun the Post

explanation.surface: A writer is the brother of a postman named Shaun.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'Penman' is a nickname in Joyce's Finnegans Wake, where the writer twin is set against his postman brother.
explanation.definitionFit: Joyce's twins in Finnegans Wake are the artist-writer and Shaun the Post, his rival brother.

clue.text: Extra rex as wayward operatic king

indicators.note: wayward means straying from the right path, so these letters go off in a new order

explanation.surface: An extra king, Latin rex, behaves in a wayward fashion on the opera stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wayward' rearranges EXTRA REX AS. The Persian king is the hero of Thomas Arne's opera of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Persian ruler is the title role of Arne's 1762 English opera.
